task.problem:
Construct a uniform deterministic algorithm with the following guarantee.

Given a vector $w\in\mathbb R^d$, where $d\geq1$, and an integer $N\geq2$, construct $\bar w\in\mathbb Z^d$ such that

$$
\operatorname{sgn}(w^\top x)=\operatorname{sgn}(\bar w^\top x)
\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb Z^d\text{ with }\|x\|_1<N.
$$

Here $\|x\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^d|x_i|$ and the sign takes the values $-1,0,1$. Zero inner products must be preserved exactly.

Every coefficient must have signed binary encoding length

$$
\max_{1\leq i\leq d}\ell(\bar w_i)=O(d\log_2 N),
\qquad \ell(z)=1+\lceil\log_2(1+|z|)\rceil.
$$

The implied constant must be absolute, uniformly in $d,N,w$, including when $N$ is fixed. A bound such as $O(d^2+d\log N)$ or $O(d\log d+d\log N)$ does not meet this target.

The algorithm must use $\operatorname{poly}(d,\log N)$ exact arithmetic operations and comparisons, independently of the magnitude or precision of $w$. Real inputs are accessed through exact arithmetic and comparisons. On rational inputs, where every coordinate of $w$ is a binary-encoded numerator and denominator and $N$ is binary encoded, all intermediate encoding lengths must remain polynomial in the total binary input length. The algorithm and the operation bound must be uniform in the dimension.

A determinant argument gives the existence of sign-equivalent integer weights with $O(d\log N)$ bits per coefficient. The target is an efficient construction with the stated computational guarantees. A prior construction achieves $O(d^2+d\log N)$ bits. Any valid mathematical approach is allowed.
task.completionCriteria:
Prove the requested constructive theorem with a complete rigorous argument under exactly the supplied hypotheses. Give a uniform deterministic algorithm and establish all of the following: preservation of all three signs for every integer vector with $\|x\|_1<N$, the per-coefficient bound $O(d\log_2 N)$ with an absolute constant, a $\operatorname{poly}(d,\log N)$ exact-arithmetic-and-comparison operation bound independent of the magnitude and precision of $w$, and polynomial intermediate encoding lengths on rational inputs.

Completion requires all these guarantees simultaneously. A nonconstructive size bound, a randomized construction, a fixed-dimension algorithm, an algorithm whose operation count depends on the encoding length of $w$, or a bound with an additional $d^2$ or $d\log d$ term does not complete the task. Keep useful partial results and failed approaches in the mathematical notes without presenting them as a solution. Establish the exact statements and hypotheses of any external results used.

notes.summary: An implemented affine-margin relaxation produces a bounded integer dead-zone statistic for all short signs, including zeros, whenever a bounded-height representative exists.
notes.text:
Let H>=1 and P>=1 be integers, and let W in Z^d be given. Write X_H={x in Z^d: ||x||_1<=H}. There is a uniform deterministic algorithm with the following alternative:

(A) It returns integers p in Z^d and K=2H^2 satisfying, for every x in X_H,
  W^T x>0  =>  p^T x >= 3K/2,
  W^T x=0  =>  |p^T x| <= K/2,
  W^T x<0  =>  p^T x <= -3K/2;                         (1)
with ||p||_infinity <= 16d P^2 H^3.

(B) It correctly concludes that no integer vector v of height at most P has all three signs of W on X_H.

The operation count is polynomial in d,H,P, independently of the magnitude or encoding length of W. Every intermediate number on encoded integer inputs has length polynomial in the total binary input length. In particular, the algorithm is useful when H and P are polynomially bounded parameters. It does not assert that the p in (A) itself preserves zeros.

1. TWO STRICT AFFINE LABELS REPLACE EACH TERNARY LABEL.
For every x in X_H and b in {-1,1}, define
  s(x,b)=sgn(2W^T x+b).
This sign is never zero, because W is integral. If v is a height-P integer representative with all three original signs, then
  s(x,b)(2v^T x+b)>=1                                (2)
for every such pair. In particular, zeros of W produce two opposite strict affine labels, rather than zero-labelled constraints.

We seek a real c satisfying
  s(x,b)(c^T x+b)>=1/2                              (3)
for all pairs. Use the fixed denominator K=2H^2, maintain c=p/K, and initialize p=0. Whenever (3) fails, update
  p <- p+s(x,b)x.                                    (4)
After T=16dP^2H^2 updates, stop and report (B) if no successful termination has occurred.

Suppose the height-P representative v exists, and put c_*=2v. For a violated pair, (2)-(3) give
  s(x,b)(c-c_*)^T x < -1/2.
Writing eta=1/K, the update therefore satisfies
  ||c+eta s(x,b)x-c_*||_2^2
    < ||c-c_*||_2^2-eta+eta^2 H^2
     =||c-c_*||_2^2-1/(4H^2).
The initial squared distance is at most 4dP^2. Thus T updates would make this nonnegative quantity strictly negative. The failure report is consequently sound. Each update changes every coordinate of p by at most H, proving the stated height bound whether or not the promise holds.

If no pair violates (3), take b=-1 when W^T x>0 and b=1 when W^T x<0. This gives the two outer inequalities in (1). When W^T x=0, the two labels for b=1 and b=-1 give the central inequality. This proves (A).

2. FINDING A VIOLATED PAIR WITHOUT ENUMERATING X_H.
At a current integer p, use a finite dynamic program. A path consists of at most H moves chosen from {+e_i,-e_i}. Its endpoint is an integer x of l1 norm at most H, and every x in X_H is an endpoint of such a path. At layer h and integer state t=p^T x, store both the minimum and maximum possible W^T x, with endpoint witnesses. There are at most 2H||p||_infinity+1 possible states per layer. The transitions are
  (h,t) -> (h+1,t+epsilon p_i),
with W-cost epsilon W_i, for epsilon in {-1,1}. Ordinary min-plus and max-plus recurrence computes both extrema. Paths with coordinate cancellations cause no problem: they still have endpoints in X_H. Conversely, the union of all layers contains every required endpoint.

For each reachable state t and b in {-1,1}, the candidate affine value t/K+b is fixed. A violation with positive s exists precisely when
  t/K+b<1/2 and 2 max(W^T x)+b>0.
A violation with negative s exists precisely when
  t/K+b>-1/2 and 2 min(W^T x)+b<0.
The stored extremizing witness supplies the update. If neither test succeeds in any state, (3) holds everywhere. Fixed scan orders and fixed dynamic-programming tie rules make the procedure deterministic.

The known bound T H on ||p||_infinity makes every state range polynomial in d,H,P. There are at most T dynamic-programming calls. All operations are exact arithmetic and comparisons. The W-dependent values are sums of at most H signed input coordinates; no rounding, binary extraction, or iteration depending on the size of W is performed. Their encoding lengths, as well as those of p, K, counters, and witnesses, have the stated bounds.

INTERPRETATION AND LIMITATION. At success, all three original labels are exactly recoverable from one bounded integer statistic:
  positive iff p^T x>=K,
  negative iff p^T x<=-K,
  zero iff -K<p^T x<K.                               (5)
There is a gap between these thresholds and the actual values in (1). Although c uses an affine anchor literally equal to one during learning, the integral pair is (p,K), not (p,1). Thus p must NOT be returned as a three-sign representative. The next note supplies a separate, implemented exact-zero restoration from the finite-state label description (5).

correctness.report: The strict affine labels correctly encode all three original signs. Under the height-P promise, each violated constraint decreases squared distance by strictly more than 1/(4H^2), making the stated update cutoff sound. The dynamic program correctly detects violations using extrema at each state, including those caused by zero-labelled rows. State counts, coefficient bounds, and individual encoding-length bounds follow as claimed. The limitation concerning exact zeros is correctly stated.

notes.summary: A finite-state sign statistic permits determinant-size exact compression by a uniform vertex walk; one-dimensional parametric dynamic programming removes any operation-count dependence on the starting integer vector.
notes.text:
FINITE-STATE LABEL COMPRESSION THEOREM. Let H>=1 and K>=1 be integers, and let p,W in Z^d. Put A=||p||_infinity. Suppose that for every x in X_H={x in Z^d:||x||_1<=H}, the three signs of W^T x are described exactly by
  positive iff p^T x>=K,
  negative iff p^T x<=-K,
  zero iff -K<p^T x<K.                               (1)
There is a uniform deterministic algorithm returning q in Z^d with all three signs of W on X_H and
  ||q||_infinity <= d H^(d-1).                       (2)
It uses polynomial(d,H,A+1,log(K+1)) exact arithmetic operations and comparisons, independently of the magnitude and encoding length of W. On encoded integer inputs, all intermediate individual encoding lengths are polynomial in the total binary input length. The algorithm needs no implicit separation oracle: all its searches are implemented below.

The case W=0 is returned directly. Assume henceforth W!=0. The condition (1) is a semantic promise. It is supplied, with a stronger gap, by n1, but no result of n1 is needed in the proof of this theorem.

1. A FINITE-STATE LINEAR-OPTIMIZATION SUBROUTINE.
For any real objective a in R^d, dynamic programming over at most H signed coordinate moves computes the minimum of a^T x in each state s=p^T x and each path length h<=H, together with an endpoint witness. Each layer has at most 2HA+1 states. The transition cost of epsilon e_i is epsilon a_i. The union of the layers represents exactly X_H: cancellations only give another allowed endpoint. Thus selecting states s>=K implements
  Min_+(a)=min{a^T x:x in X_H, p^T x>=K}.             (3)
Selecting states |s|<K implements minimization over the zero-labelled set X_0. Maximization is obtained by negating the objective. The number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is polynomial in d,H,A+1, without dependence on the objective's magnitude or precision. Unreachable states are stored as a Boolean flag, not as an infinite arithmetic value.

2. COMPUTE THE EXACT ZERO SPAN.
Maintain a list of independent rows from X_0, initially empty, and let E be their real span. Compute an integer basis h_1,...,h_r of E-perpendicular by rational elimination and minors. For each h_i maximize h_i^T x over X_0 by the preceding dynamic program. The set X_0 is symmetric. Consequently, if any h_i has a nonzero pairing with some row in X_0, its maximum is strictly positive. The maximizing row is outside E; add it and restart. If all maxima are zero, every row in X_0 lies in E, and the zero span is complete.

There are at most d rank increases and at most d objective tests per increase. Each selected row has l1 norm at most H. Minor formulas can supply nullspace vectors with entries bounded by H^d: determinants of r-row matrices are bounded by H^r, since row Euclidean norms are at most H and Gram-Schmidt gives the product-of-row-norm determinant bound. This also bounds all relevant integer encoding lengths. In particular, E contains e_i whenever W_i=0, and W annihilates E.

3. A FEASIBLE VERTEX WALK IN THE ORIGINAL d VARIABLES.
Consider the polyhedron
  F={z in E-perpendicular : x^T z>=1 for every x in X_+},
where X_+={x in X_H:p^T x>=K}. The integer vector W belongs to F, by (1). Start at z=W. Keep the independent zero-span equations and any positive equations x^T z=1 discovered during the walk as an active row list.

If the active rank is less than d, choose a nonzero integer u annihilated by these rows. It can be chosen by minors with ||u||_infinity<=H^(d-1). Put c_i=sgn(W_i), and choose the sign of u so that c^T u<=0. For W_i=0, u_i=0 because e_i belongs to E. Since u!=0, there must therefore be an index with W_i!=0 and c_i u_i<0. The coordinate row c_i e_i belongs to X_+. It follows that moving along z+t u remains feasible for precisely an interval
  0<=t<=t_*,
where t_* is finite and
  t_*=min_{x in X_+, x^T u<0} (x^T z-1)/(-x^T u).   (4)
Zero is allowed as the minimum. A minimizing row is independent of the old active rows, because it has a nonzero pairing with u. Find such a row by the implemented procedure in Step 4, move to z+t_*u, and add it to the active list. The point remains feasible and the active rank increases. There are at most d moves, including possible zero-length moves.

At termination let R be the nonsingular d by d matrix of selected active rows, and let b have entry zero for zero equations and entry one for positive equations. Then z=R^(-1)b. Return
  q=|det R|z.
It is integral, annihilates every required zero row, and has strictly positive pairing with every row in X_+. Negative rows are negatives of positive rows. Thus all three signs are correct.

For every coordinate, the adjugate formula expands q_i into at most d signed (d-1)-row minors. Each remaining row has Euclidean norm at most H, even after a column is deleted. Therefore |q_i|<=dH^(d-1), proving (2). The construction never includes a long objective row in R. This is important for avoiding an additional dimension-dependent coefficient loss.

4. EXACT MINIMUM-RATIO SEARCH BY ONE-DIMENSIONAL PARAMETRIC DYNAMIC PROGRAMMING.
This is the pivotal computational step. It avoids a bisection bound involving the encoding length of z or W.

For the current feasible z and chosen u, ordinary evaluation of (3) at z+rho u decides feasibility at any rho>=0:
  z+rho u in F iff Min_+(z+rho u)>=1.
Because the feasible interval along this direction is [0,t_*], this test decides rho<=t_* exactly, including the endpoint.

Now run the dynamic program minimizing (z+t u)^T x, symbolically at the right-hand germ t=t_*+0. Store at each state an endpoint x; its symbolic cost is the affine function
  f_x(t)=z^T x+t u^T x.
Every comparison is between two affine functions. Write their difference as alpha+beta t. If beta=0, its sign is determined directly, with a fixed tie rule when alpha=0. Otherwise its root is rho=-alpha/beta. If rho<0, then t_*+0 lies to its right. If rho>=0, run the ordinary feasibility dynamic program at rho. A feasible rho means rho<=t_*, so again the right-hand germ lies to the right of the root; an infeasible rho means rho>t_*, so it lies to its left. Multiplying this side information by sgn(beta) resolves the symbolic comparison.

Each comparison thus uses at most one ordinary dynamic-programming call. No symbolic simulation is used inside those calls. All comparisons agree with evaluation at t_*+epsilon for all sufficiently small positive epsilon, since only finitely many affine functions occur. The final endpoint a therefore minimizes f_x at this right-hand germ over X_+.

At t_*, every f_x is at least one, and some row has f_x(t_*)=1 and negative slope. Consequently the right-hand minimizing endpoint satisfies
  a^T z+t_* a^T u=1,  a^T u<0.
Thus it is a minimizing row for (4), and t_*=(a^T z-1)/(-a^T u) is now computed by exact arithmetic. This proves the minimum-ratio procedure, even when t_*=0 or several rows become tight simultaneously.

If an ordinary dynamic-programming call has T polynomially bounded comparisons and arithmetic operations, this symbolic version has polynomially many operations, for example O(T^2) times the cost of storing and pairing endpoint vectors. Its operation count contains no logarithm of the magnitude or precision of z.

5. ENCODING BOUNDS.
The zero-span and active rows are bounded integer vectors. Integer null directions obtained by minors have polynomial encoding length in d and log(H+1). Every successful update is
  z <- (I-u a^T/(a^T u))z+u/(a^T u),
with 0<|a^T u|<=H^d. There are at most d updates. Hence all z coordinates have encoding lengths polynomial in the length of W and in d,log(H+1).

In a symbolic comparison, alpha=z^T(x-y) and beta=u^T(x-y), where ||x-y||_1<=2H. Thus beta is an integer of magnitude at most 2H^d. Every root and every numerical objective z+rho u has polynomial encoding length. Dynamic-programming values may be recomputed as objective pairings with the stored bounded endpoint, so a long recurrence does not introduce additional denominators. All determinants, adjugates, and final coordinates satisfy the same polynomial-length requirement.

This proves the stated uniform construction. Its remaining non-polynomial dependence relative to the original task is on the NUMBER of states, namely the magnitudes H and A, not on W's precision.

correctness.report: The finite-state optimization and zero-span computation are valid. Coordinate constraints ensure every chosen walk direction encounters a finite boundary; a returned negative-slope row increases active rank, including for zero-length moves. The right-hand-germ simulation correctly resolves comparisons using feasibility queries, including roots equal to the boundary time. Final determinant scaling preserves zeros and strict signs and gives the bound d H^(d-1). The bounded integer slopes and at most d updates establish the claimed arithmetic and encoding bounds.

notes.summary: An implemented guarded progress branch finds determinant-height objective-positive conformal rays from quantized near-zero hulls; it can output horizontal recession rays without an implicit separation oracle, but a geometric family shows the branch is not universal.
notes.text:
QUANTIZED-HULL RAY ALGORITHM. Let H>=1 and B>=1 be integers. Given real w,h in R^d and an integer threshold L>=H, the following deterministic procedure either returns failure or constructs an integer u with
  sgn(w^T x) u^T x>=0 when w^T x!=0,
  u^T x=0 when w^T x=0,
  h^T u>0,
  ||u||_infinity<=H^(d-1)                            (1)
for every integer x with ||x||_1<=H. All its searches are implemented. The operation count is polynomial in d,H,B, independently of the magnitudes and precision of w,h. Rational intermediate encoding lengths are polynomial in the total input length. A successful output need not preserve every strict sign: it is a genuinely closed-conformal ray.

The procedure succeeds whenever the directly computed projection tests below pass. These tests can be tried for every relevant threshold in polynomial(d,H,B) operations. Thus this is an implemented, certifiable progress branch, not an assumed ray oracle.

1. QUANTIZE AND COMPUTE A GENUINE SHORT-ROW HULL.
If w=0, report failure. Otherwise normalize
  a=w/||w||_infinity.
Round each coordinate of Ba to a nearest integer, with a fixed tie rule, obtaining p. Then
  ||p||_infinity<=B,
  ||a-p/B||_infinity<=1/(2B).                        (2)
All rounding is on the known interval [-B,B], and uses bounded binary search.

Let E be the real span of the integer rows
  Z_L={x:||x||_1<=H, |p^T x|<=L}.
Compute an integer basis for E consisting of rows from Z_L. This is exactly the span-finding procedure of n2, with threshold L+1: dynamic programming on the states p^T x optimizes each nullspace direction over Z_L, adding an independent witness whenever the maximum is positive. Each chosen basis row has l1 norm at most H. The state range is bounded by HB, so this entire step is polynomial in d,H,B.

Every original zero row belongs to E. Indeed, a^T x=0 and (2) imply |p^T x|<=H/2<=L.

Compute the Euclidean projection
  r=proj_E a,  q=a-r.
All projectors are obtained by rational linear algebra on the selected bounded integer basis; the only real data are linear combinations of the original input.

2. THE COMPUTABLE SUCCESS TEST.
Require both
  H||r||_infinity < (L+1-H/2)/B,                     (3)
  h^T q>0.                                         (4)
If either fails, report failure. No square roots are needed in these tests.

If x is a required row outside E, then |p^T x|>=L+1, because every row in the band was included in E. Consequently
  sgn(p^T x) q^T x
    >= (L+1)/B-H/(2B)-H||r||_infinity>0.             (5)
The same inequality without the last term shows that a^T x has the sign of p^T x. Therefore q has the strict original sign on every required row outside E, and vanishes on every row in E. In particular q is closed-conformal with w. Condition (4) ensures it is a useful nonzero direction rather than the zero vector.

One must not merely clear the denominators of q: for arbitrary real inputs q need not be rational, and even for rational inputs that could pay for the original precision. The next step replaces q by a determinant-height integer direction using the finite-state description.

3. AN IMPLEMENTED INTEGER RAY WALK.
Define
  Y={x in Z^d:||x||_1<=H, p^T x>=L+1},
  C={z in E-perpendicular : x^T z>=0 for every x in Y}.
The cone C is contained in the original closed conformal cone. For an original positive row outside E, (5) implies that it belongs to Y; rows inside E are annihilated. Original negative rows are handled by negation, and original zero rows belong to E.

Furthermore, C lies in the coordinate orthant of q, with coordinates zero wherever q has coordinate zero. To see this, if q_i=0, then e_i must belong to E: otherwise (5), applied to the required coordinate row, would make q_i nonzero. Hence every z in C has z_i=0 there. If q_i!=0, then e_i is outside E; its p sign is the q sign, and the corresponding oriented coordinate row belongs to Y.

Put c_i=sgn(q_i). On C, c^T z=||z||_1. Thus the section
  C intersect {c^T z=1}
is bounded. It contains z_0=q/(c^T q), with h^T z_0>0.

Perform a feasible vertex walk in this section. The active equations initially consist of the selected basis of E and c^T z=1. When their rank is less than d, choose a nonzero integer direction v annihilating all active rows, and orient it so that h^T v>=0. Some oriented coordinate inequality has negative slope: v vanishes in the fixed zero coordinates, c^T v=0, and v!=0. Hence there is a finite first boundary time
  t_*=min_{x in Y, x^T v<0} x^T z/(-x^T v).
The minimum can be zero.

Compute an exact minimizing row by n2's one-dimensional parametric dynamic program. Here the feasibility test is
  min_{x in Y} (z+rho v)^T x>=0,
with right-hand side zero rather than one. The minimization is the same finite-state dynamic program indexed by p^T x. Feasibility along the ray is exactly the interval [0,t_*]. Symbolically minimizing at t_*+0 therefore resolves each affine comparison by at most one ordinary feasibility call, exactly as proved in n2. The returned row has negative slope and is tight at t_*. Move to z+t_*v and add this independent row to the active set.

At most d rank increases occur. Objective h never decreases, so it stays strictly positive. At termination choose a nonsingular active row matrix R with c as its first row. Every other row is homogeneous and has l1 norm at most H: it is either one of the selected rows spanning E or a row from Y. The right-hand side is e_1. Return
  u=|det R| R^(-1)e_1.
It is an integer point of C with h^T u>0. Each coordinate is, up to sign, a (d-1)-row minor after deleting the first row c. The product-of-row-norm determinant bound gives ||u||_infinity<=H^(d-1). In particular the possibly dense section row c contributes no d log d loss. This proves every assertion in (1).

4. COMPUTATIONAL DETAILS AND THRESHOLD SEARCH.
The dynamic-programming state count is polynomial in H and B. All hull bases consist of actual short rows. Null directions in the vertex walk are given by minors of these rows and the bounded row c. The number of walk steps is at most d, and the symbolic minimum-ratio implementation has a polynomial number of ordinary dynamic-programming calls, with no bisection depending on the precision of q.

For rational data, the initial projection and normalization have polynomial encoding lengths. Each walk step is a bounded rational linear transformation of the current point; objective comparisons use h only to choose a sign. As in n2, numerical dynamic-programming objectives at comparison roots are pairings of the current point with bounded endpoint vectors, divided by parameter-bounded integer slopes. Recomputing such pairings from stored endpoints prevents uncontrolled denominator recurrences. These observations establish the rational-workspace and precision-independent operation claims.

If L>=B, every coordinate row belongs to Z_L, so E=R^d and (4) fails. Thus only L in {H,...,B-1} need be tried. Literal enumeration of these thresholds is polynomial in B and adds no unresolved search. A fixed budget B polynomial in d and log N, together with an initial guard that H=N-1 is polynomially bounded in those parameters, turns this into a uniform polynomial-operation branch for the original problem. Inputs failing the guard can be passed immediately to another branch.

5. HORIZONTAL OUTPUTS FOR UNIT-ANCHOR INPUTS.
Apply the construction in dimension D=d+1 to V=(W,1), with max_i |W_i|>2B. After normalization, the anchor coordinate rounds to zero. Its coordinate row therefore lies in every Z_L, so every returned u has anchor coordinate exactly zero. If the objective is (W-proj_F W,0), where F is a previously collected ordinary-coordinate span, condition (4) and the final objective guarantee certify that a successful ordinary-coordinate ray lies outside F. This supplies an actual horizontal conformal escape on the passing branch. It does not silently replace anchor one by an arbitrary positive anchor, and it never claims that a horizontal ray alone is a final representative.

6. WHY THIS BRANCH IS NOT UNIVERSAL.
There is a simple obstruction even at H=4. Take
  w_i=(5/2)^i,  i=0,...,d-1.
For every nonzero integer closed-conformal u, coordinate tests give u_i>=0, while the required positive rows
  e_(i+1)-2e_i,  3e_i-e_(i+1)
force
  2u_i<=u_(i+1)<=3u_i.
A zero in any coordinate would force every coordinate to be zero. Hence u_0>=1 and u_(d-1)>=2^(d-1).

After normalization, a_0=(2/5)^(d-1). If B a_0<1/2, the quantized coordinate p_0 is zero, so e_0 belongs to every band hull E considered above. Every output of the ray walk would then have u_0=0, impossible for a nonzero closed-conformal ray. Thus, for every polynomial choice of B and sufficiently large d, no threshold can pass both success tests on this family. This is an obstruction to the new guarded branch, not to the requested compressor: the displayed rational input already has a target-bit integer representative by clearing its powers-of-two denominators.

STATUS. The quantized-hull construction is a genuinely implemented source of target-height conformal progress, including horizontal recession progress under a directly testable condition. It does not guarantee that the test succeeds until a small residual is reached. Combining successful calls with existing completion mechanisms is safe, but no universal termination or sharp-size theorem follows. The unrestricted constructive task remains unresolved.

correctness.report: Conditional on the declared finite-state procedures, the projection tests correctly certify conformity outside the computed hull and annihilation inside it. Coordinate rows establish the asserted orthant containment and bounded section. The objective-monotone vertex walk has finite boundary times and strictly increasing active rank; the parametric search applies with right-hand side zero. Cofactors exclude the section row, giving precisely H^(d-1). Computational bounds, the horizontal-output observation, and the geometric-progression obstruction are valid. No universal success guarantee is asserted.
